questions.stem: Which of the following best defines absolute poverty?
options: Income insufficient to afford the basic necessities of life, measured against a fixed standard
Income well below the average in a particular society
Income below the median in a country
Income that has fallen over the last year
questions.why: The threshold is fixed in real terms, which is why absolute poverty can in principle be eliminated.
whyNot: That is relative poverty.
That is a relative measure.
A falling income is not a poverty definition.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines relative poverty?
options: Income well below the average in a particular society
Income below a fixed international threshold
Income insufficient for basic necessities
Income that is unstable from year to year
questions.why: It is really a measure of inequality at the bottom of the distribution rather than of deprivation.
whyNot: That is absolute poverty.
That is absolute poverty.
That is income volatility.

questions.stem: Which type of poverty can in principle be eliminated?
options: Absolute poverty, because the threshold is fixed
Relative poverty, because it is defined against the average
Both, given enough growth
Neither, under any circumstances
questions.why: If every income doubled, absolute poverty would fall sharply and relative poverty would not change at all.
whyNot: A measure defined against the average cannot be eliminated.
Relative poverty cannot be, by construction.
Absolute poverty can be, and has fallen dramatically in some regions.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a poverty trap?
options: A situation in which low income prevents the saving, investment or education needed to raise it
A benefit system that pays too much to those in work
A tax on the incomes of the poorest households
An area of a country with unusually high unemployment
questions.why: It also refers to high effective marginal tax and benefit withdrawal rates that remove the incentive to earn more.
whyNot: That would reduce poverty rather than trap people in it.
That is a regressive tax.
That is a regional problem.

questions.stem: Why can measured relative poverty fall during a recession?
options: Median income falls, so the relative poverty line falls with it
Benefits automatically rise faster than prices
The poorest gain employment during a recession
Relative poverty is not measured during a recession
questions.why: A measure that improves when the economy collapses needs careful reading.
whyNot: Benefits may be uprated, but that is not the mechanism.
Unemployment rises among the poorest in a recession.
It continues to be measured.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most powerful force reducing absolute poverty?
options: Economic growth, provided its benefits reach the poorest
Relative poverty measurement
Higher indirect taxes on necessities
A rise in the exchange rate
questions.why: Growth concentrated in a capital-intensive extractive sector may raise GDP substantially and leave absolute poverty almost unchanged, so the pattern of growth matters.
whyNot: Measurement does not change outcomes.
That raises the price of necessities for the poorest.
The exchange rate is not a poverty instrument.

questions.stem: Why can growth raise relative poverty while reducing absolute poverty?
options: Growth concentrated among higher earners widens the distribution while raising incomes at the bottom
Growth always reduces both measures equally
Growth always raises both measures
Relative poverty is unaffected by growth
questions.why: A policy can reduce one measure while raising the other, which is exactly what an evaluation question rewards.
whyNot: They can move in opposite directions.
Absolute poverty generally falls with growth.
It depends directly on how income is distributed.

questions.stem: What is the main trade-off between means-tested and universal benefits?
options: Means-testing targets better but creates worse incentives and lower take-up
Universal benefits target better and cost less
Means-testing is always cheaper to administer
Universal benefits create a poverty trap
questions.why: Universal benefits reach everyone and cost more and are less redistributive per dollar spent.
whyNot: Universal benefits reach everyone, so they target less precisely.
Means-testing requires assessment and so is more expensive to administer.
The poverty trap arises from benefit withdrawal under means-testing.

questions.stem: Why may education fail to reduce poverty in the short run?
options: It takes a generation, and families may be unable to forgo a child's earnings
Education has no effect on productivity
Educated workers earn less than uneducated ones
Education raises the birth rate
questions.why: It also delivers little if there are no jobs for the newly skilled, in which case the outcome is emigration.
whyNot: It raises human capital and therefore productivity.
Returns to education are generally positive and substantial.
It tends to reduce the birth rate.

questions.stem: Why is conflict identified first in any answer where the source mentions it?
options: It destroys infrastructure, human capital and institutions, so no other policy functions
It is the easiest constraint to remove
It affects only military spending
It raises poverty only temporarily
questions.why: It displaces populations, halts investment, diverts spending and disrupts food production, and the effects persist for decades.
whyNot: It is among the hardest.
It affects every aspect of the economy.
The effects are long lasting.

questions.stem: Why is tied aid worth less than its face value?
options: It must be spent on goods or services from the donor country, which may not be the cheapest
It must be repaid with interest
It cannot be spent on infrastructure
It is paid in the donor's currency
questions.why: Aid can also be lost to corruption, create dependency, displace domestic production and be volatile.
whyNot: Aid is a grant, unlike a loan.
It can fund infrastructure, subject to the tying condition.
The currency is not the problem; the restriction on suppliers is.

questions.stem: Why can raising the tax-free threshold reduce poverty?
options: It raises the post-tax income of the lowest earners directly
It raises the marginal tax rate on the poorest
It reduces government spending on benefits automatically
It raises indirect taxes on necessities
questions.why: Cutting indirect taxes on necessities has a similar effect, and both must be financed.
whyNot: It reduces their average tax rate.
Benefit spending is a separate decision.
That would worsen poverty.

questions.stem: Why does structural change raise poverty in the short run and reduce it later?
options: It destroys livelihoods faster than it creates replacements, while raising average productivity over time
It always reduces total output
It only affects the agricultural sector
It raises poverty permanently
questions.why: Those displaced frequently lack the skills to follow the work, which is why the transition is painful.
whyNot: It raises average productivity and output over time.
It affects all sectors.
Long-run incomes generally rise.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the international poverty line?
options: It says nothing about how far below the line people are
It cannot be compared between countries
It is measured in local currency without adjustment
It includes non-income dimensions of poverty
questions.why: The threshold is arbitrary, PPP conversions are imprecise, and access to public services is ignored.
whyNot: Comparability between countries is one of its strengths.
It is measured at purchasing power parity.
It is an income measure; multidimensional measures add other dimensions.

questions.stem: Why does the effectiveness of aid depend heavily on governance?
options: Aid can be lost to corruption and misallocated where institutions are weak
Aid is only offered to well-governed countries
Governance determines the currency aid is paid in
Aid has no effect under any circumstances
questions.why: This is why aid effectiveness rather than aid volume is the live question.
whyNot: Aid is given to countries with a wide range of governance quality.
Currency is not the issue.
Its results in disease control and primary education have been substantial.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a multidimensional measure of poverty?
options: A measure combining nutrition, schooling, water, sanitation and electricity
A fixed income threshold at purchasing power parity
A percentage of median income
The Gini coefficient
questions.why: Its strength is that poverty is not only about income; its limitation is that the weights given to each dimension are a judgement.
whyNot: That is the international poverty line.
That is a relative poverty measure.
That measures inequality.
